object_types.name: Customer
object_types.definition: A person or entity that places orders, identified by a unique customer ID in the CRM system.

source_references.excerpt: A customer places an order.
Each customer has a unique customer ID in the CRM system.
In our CRM they're "customers" but the billing team calls them "clients."

object_types.name: Order
object_types.definition: A purchase order placed by exactly one customer, identified by an order number.

ambiguities.description: The transcript notes that 'Customer' (CRM) and 'Client' (billing) are treated as the same concept for modeling purposes, but the billing team applies a different definition -- someone is only a 'client' once they have actually paid. This suggests Client may actually be a subtype or state of Customer (e.g., a Customer who has made a payment) rather than a pure synonym. Should 'Client' be modeled as a distinct subtype/status rather than an alias?

source_references.excerpt: I've heard some people call customers "clients" in the billing system... they only consider someone a client once they've actually paid.

ambiguities.description: The order-product-quantity relationship is described as 'each line in the order specifies a product and a quantity,' implying an order line could be an entity in its own right (e.g., with a line number) rather than a simple ternary fact. Should 'Order Line' be modeled as an objectified entity with its own identifier, especially if the same product can appear on multiple distinct lines within one order (e.g., different batches)?

source_references.excerpt: Each line in the order specifies a product and a quantity.

ambiguities.description: No explicit statement addresses whether a Product must appear on at least one Order (mandatory participation on the Product side) or whether Products can exist unordered in a catalog with zero orders. This affects whether the Product role in 'Order contains Product with Quantity' should be mandatory.

source_references.excerpt: A product can appear in many different orders.
